prompt: In many countries, public confidence in politicians has fallen sharply in recent decades. What has caused this loss of trust? How might it be rebuilt?
essay:
Distrust of politicians is often treated as a modern pathology, but it is better understood as a rational response to two changes in how democratic politics now works. Neither requires politicians to have become worse people than they were fifty years ago, which is precisely why appeals to personal integrity have failed to repair it.

The first change is that the promises have grown while the levers have shrunk. A candidate must still campaign on housing, prices and waiting lists, yet the forces that move those things — interest rates set elsewhere, supply chains, demographic pressure building for decades — are largely beyond a single administration's reach. The result is a mismatch nobody can escape: a politician who described the constraints honestly would lose to one who did not, so almost nobody does, and every term ends with a record of undelivered commitments that looks like deceit even when it is closer to arithmetic.

The second is that the record is now complete. Everything a representative says is captured, searchable and comparable with everything they said before, while the mundane work of government — a functioning department, a bill sensibly amended in committee — leaves almost no trace. Voters are therefore assembling their judgement from a sample systematically weighted towards failure.

Any serious repair has to work on those two mechanisms rather than on manners. Independent costing of manifestos before an election would make the honest candidate competitive by making the dishonest one contestable, which is the only way that incentive changes. And governments should be required to publish, annually, a plain account of which commitments they have met, missed and abandoned. Publishing failure looks like political suicide; in practice it is the cheapest credibility available, because a promise openly written off stops being evidence of bad faith and becomes evidence that somebody is keeping score.
title: Why people no longer trust politicians
